metadata.transformation_policy: Preserve source terminology, mechanisms, implementations, use cases, references and distinctions; no outside corrections or silent reconciliation.
metadata.core_thesis: A sandbox separates running programs inside a restricted environment and controls their available resources and host access to contain failures and vulnerabilities.
metadata.relationship_semantics: Directed relationships preserve mechanism, effect, conditions, scope, implementation, containment, restriction, comparison, use, historical association and provenance.

Source claim 1
nodes.statement: Sandbox separates running programs to mitigate spread of system failures and software vulnerabilities.

nodes.label: Source claim 2
nodes.statement: Sandbox resources include storage and memory scratch space; network access, host inspection and input-device access are usually restricted.

nodes.label: Source claim 3
nodes.statement: Sandboxing can be comparable to virtualization when providing a highly controlled environment.

nodes.label: Source claim 4
nodes.statement: Sandboxing is implemented by executing software in a restricted operating-system environment.

nodes.label: Source claim 5
nodes.statement: Linux application sandboxing uses seccomp, cgroups and namespaces.

nodes.label: Source claim 6
nodes.statement: Android assigns each application its own Linux user ID for application sandboxing.

nodes.label: Source claim 7
nodes.statement: GrapheneOS hardens app sandboxing and allows sandboxing every app as described.

nodes.label: Source claim 8
nodes.statement: Apple App Sandbox is required for specified App Store apps and recommended for other signed apps.

nodes.label: Source claim 9
nodes.statement: Virtual machines emulate a complete host computer and mediate host-resource access through the emulator.

nodes.label: Source claim 10
nodes.statement: Jails restrict network access and filesystem namespace and are common in virtual hosting.

nodes.label: Source claim 11
nodes.statement: Rule-based execution controls process spawning, code injection, network access and file/registry operations.

nodes.label: Source claim 12
nodes.statement: Security researchers use sandboxing to analyze malware behavior in replicated target environments.

nodes.label: Source claim 13
nodes.statement: Google Native Client sandboxes compiled C/C++ code in browsers independently of the user's OS.

nodes.label: Source claim 14
nodes.statement: Capability systems use opaque tokens to grant specific rights and can operate at kernel or user-space levels.

nodes.label: Source claim 15
nodes.statement: Strict seccomp permits only read, write, exit and sigreturn.

nodes.label: Source claim 16
nodes.statement: HTML5 iframe sandboxing restricts embedded content.

nodes.label: Source claim 17
nodes.statement: Java virtual machines sandbox untrusted applets/code.

nodes.label: Source claim 18
nodes.statement: .NET CLR Code Access Security restricts untrusted code.

nodes.label: Source claim 19
nodes.statement: SFI isolates store, read and jump assembly instructions into memory segments.

nodes.label: Source claim 20
nodes.statement: Online judges and executable pastebins are sandbox use cases.

nodes.label: Sandbox vs virtualization
nodes.definition: Sandboxing is a security mechanism; virtualization can provide a highly controlled environment but is broader.

nodes.label: Restricted OS vs full VM
nodes.definition: A restricted process environment is distinct from a VM emulating a complete host computer.

nodes.label: Kernel mechanism vs policy
nodes.definition: seccomp/cgroups/namespaces are listed Linux building blocks; rule-based frameworks impose access policy.

nodes.label: Android UID isolation
nodes.definition: The described Android sandbox uses per-application Linux user IDs.

nodes.label: Jail vs VM
nodes.definition: A jail is characterized by network and filesystem namespace restrictions rather than full hardware emulation.

nodes.label: Capabilities vs rules
nodes.definition: Capabilities grant rights through tokens; rule-based systems assign access levels through rules.

nodes.label: OS vs instruction isolation
nodes.definition: SFI constrains native instructions to memory segments.

nodes.label: Defense vs analysis
nodes.definition: Sandboxing can contain threats and provide a controlled observation environment.

nodes.label: Restriction vs absolute denial
nodes.definition: Resources may be disallowed or heavily restricted; sandboxing is not necessarily total denial.

nodes.label: Guest vs host
nodes.definition: The sandbox boundary separates guest execution from host resources.

nodes.label: Security mechanism vs application container
nodes.definition: The source presents sandboxing as a security mechanism and does not equate it with application containerization.

nodes.label: Trusted vs untrusted code
nodes.definition: Sandboxing is especially useful for unverified/untrusted code.

nodes.label: Browser active code vs unrestricted code
nodes.definition: Native Client and iframe sandboxing show active browser code can execute under restrictions.

nodes.label: Strict vs normal syscall surface
nodes.definition: Strict seccomp exposes only four named system calls.

nodes.label: Embedded vs top-level content
nodes.definition: HTML5 sandbox specifically constrains iframe content.

nodes.label: Platform-specific mechanisms
nodes.definition: Linux, Android, Apple, Windows, browser and language runtimes use different mechanisms.

nodes.label: Virtual-hosting jail
nodes.definition: Jails are noted as common in virtual hosting.

nodes.label: Fine-grained capability control
nodes.definition: Capability systems are explicitly described as fine-grained sandboxing.

nodes.label: Sandbox means full VM
nodes.correction: The source treats VMs as one implementation and lists many non-VM mechanisms.

nodes.label: Sandbox blocks everything
nodes.correction: The source describes controlled, disallowed, or heavily restricted resources.

nodes.label: Sandbox is only for malware
nodes.correction: Online judges and pastebins are explicit non-malware use cases.

nodes.label: Every app sandbox requires a VM
nodes.correction: Android's described mechanism uses Linux user IDs.

nodes.label: Jail equals VM
nodes.correction: The source characterizes jails through network and filesystem namespace restrictions.

nodes.label: Capabilities equal rule policies
nodes.correction: Tokens/capabilities grant specific rights; rule systems assign access levels.

nodes.label: Sandboxing is only OS-level
nodes.correction: The source includes browser, runtime, capability and instruction-level mechanisms.

nodes.label: SFI is just process isolation
nodes.correction: SFI isolates specified native-code instruction effects into memory segments.

relationships.qualification: when providing a highly controlled environment
source describes a low-mode process running

relationships.scope: process start/spawn, code injection, network, file/registry read-write

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Execution occurs inside a restricted environment with controlled resources and host-facing operations.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Reduces the ability of failures and vulnerabilities to spread.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Strength depends on enforcement of the sandbox boundary.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Network, host inspection, input devices and other resources are disallowed or heavily restricted.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Limits the guest's ability to harm the host.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: System-call filtering is one of the Linux kernel mechanisms used for application sandboxing.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Reduces the kernel interface exposed to a sandboxed application.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The source explicitly combines it with cgroups and namespaces.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: A broader syscall surface increases available operations.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: cgroups are a Linux kernel feature used as part of application sandboxing.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Source does not specify a complete cgroup policy.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Linux namespaces are a kernel feature used as part of application sandboxing.
Each application receives its own Linux user ID.
Adds hardening to Android app sandboxing and permits sandboxing every app as described.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Source contrasts this with stock Android.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: A virtual machine emulates a complete host computer so a conventional guest OS can boot and run.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Guest execution is separated from native host execution.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Host-resource access is mediated through the emulator.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Direct native host access bypasses the described mediation.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Host resources are accessed through the emulator rather than natively.
Network-access restrictions and a restricted filesystem namespace define the jail boundary.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Source notes common use in virtual hosting.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Predetermined rules govern process spawning, code injection, network use and file/registry access.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: SELinux and AppArmor are cited implementations.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: A sandbox mimics or replicates a target desktop and contains malware execution.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Researchers can evaluate malware behavior without exposing the real target host.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: A nonrepresentative environment may not reproduce target behavior.
Can operate at kernel or user-space levels.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Only read(), write(), exit(), and sigreturn() are permitted.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: The allowlist is exactly as stated in the source.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Operations requiring other calls cannot execute.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: The HTML5 sandbox attribute restricts iframe content.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Embedded content runs under a constrained browser context.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Removing the attribute removes those restrictions.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Store, read and jump assembly instructions are sandboxed into isolated memory segments.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Constrains untrusted native code to designated memory regions.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Mechanism described as Software Fault Isolation.
rich_semantic_relationships.inverse_or_converse: Broader instruction reach weakens the isolation.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Contest programs execute in a constrained server environment.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: Submitted programs can be tested while limiting impact on the judge host.
rich_semantic_relationships.conditions: Source explicitly lists online judges as a use case.

rich_semantic_relationships.mechanism: Pasted code snippets execute on a server inside a sandbox.
rich_semantic_relationships.effect: User-supplied code can run while limiting server impact.
